pages.title: Aspirin for primary prevention of cardiovascular events

claims.text: In a collaborative meta-analysis of individual participant data from six primary prevention trials (95,000 individuals at low average risk, 660,000 person-years, 3554 serious vascular events), aspirin allocation yielded a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% aspirin vs 0.57% control per year, p=0.0001), due mainly to a reduction of about a fifth in non-fatal myocardial infarction.

evidence.quote: In the primary prevention trials, aspirin allocation yielded a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events (0.51% aspirin vs 0.57% control per year, p=0.0001), due mainly to a reduction of about a fifth in non-fatal myocardial infarction (0.18%vs 0.23% per year, p<0.0001).

claims.text: In the same meta-analysis, the net effect of aspirin on stroke was not significant and vascular mortality did not differ significantly.

evidence.quote: The net effect on stroke was not significant (0.20%vs 0.21% per year, p=0.4: haemorrhagic stroke 0.04%vs 0.03%, p=0.05; other stroke 0.16%vs 0.18% per year, p=0.08). Vascular mortality did not differ significantly (0.19%vs 0.19% per year, p=0.7).

claims.text: In a systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 trials randomizing 164,225 participants with no known cardiovascular disease, aspirin use was associated with significant reductions in the composite cardiovascular outcome compared with no aspirin (57.1 per 10,000 participant-years with aspirin and 61.4 per 10,000 participant-years with no aspirin; HR, 0.89 [95% credible interval, 0.84-0.95]; absolute risk reduction, 0.38% [95% CI, 0.20%-0.55%]; number needed to treat, 265).

evidence.quote: A total of 13 trials randomizing 164 225 participants with 1 050 511 participant-years of follow-up were included. … Aspirin use was associated with significant reductions in the composite cardiovascular outcome compared with no aspirin (57.1 per 10 000 participant-years with aspirin and 61.4 per 10 000 participant-years with no aspirin) (hazard ratio [HR], 0.89 [95% credible interval, 0.84-0.95]; absolute risk reduction, 0.38% [95% CI, 0.20%-0.55%]; number needed to treat, 265).

claims.text: In ARRIVE, which enrolled patients at moderate estimated risk of a first cardiovascular event, the primary composite endpoint occurred in 269 (4.29%) patients in the aspirin group versus 281 (4.48%) in the placebo group (HR 0.96; 95% CI 0.81-1.13; p=0.6038).

evidence.quote: In the intention-to-treat analysis, the primary endpoint occurred in 269 (4·29%) patients in the aspirin group versus 281 (4·48%) patients in the placebo group (hazard ratio [HR] 0·96; 95% CI 0·81-1·13; p=0·6038).

claims.text: In the Japanese Primary Prevention Project, the 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate was not significantly different between aspirin and no aspirin (2.77% [95% CI, 2.40%-3.20%] for aspirin vs 2.96% [95% CI, 2.58%-3.40%] for no aspirin; HR, 0.94 [95% CI, 0.77-1.15]; P = .54).

evidence.quote: The 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate was not significantly different between the groups (2.77% [95% CI, 2.40%-3.20%] for aspirin vs 2.96% [95% CI, 2.58%-3.40%] for no aspirin; hazard ratio [HR], 0.94 [95% CI, 0.77-1.15]; P = .54).

claims.text: In ASPREE, among older adults without cardiovascular disease, the rate of cardiovascular disease was 10.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.3 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (HR, 0.95; 95% CI, 0.83 to 1.08).

evidence.quote: After a median of 4.7 years of follow-up, the rate of cardiovascular disease was 10.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.3 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.95; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.83 to 1.08).

claims.text: In ASCEND, among adults with diabetes but no evident cardiovascular disease, serious vascular events occurred in a significantly lower percentage of participants in the aspirin group than in the placebo group (658 participants [8.5%] vs. 743 [9.6%]; rate ratio, 0.88; 95% CI, 0.79 to 0.97; P=0.01).

evidence.quote: During a mean follow-up of 7.4 years, serious vascular events occurred in a significantly lower percentage of participants in the aspirin group than in the placebo group (658 participants [8.5%] vs. 743 [9.6%]; rate ratio, 0.88; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.79 to 0.97; P=0.01).

claims.text: In the collaborative meta-analysis of primary prevention trials, aspirin allocation increased major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds (0.10% vs 0.07% per year, p<0.0001).

evidence.quote: Aspirin allocation increased major gastrointestinal and extracranial bleeds (0.10%vs 0.07% per year, p<0.0001), and the main risk factors for coronary disease were also risk factors for bleeding.

claims.text: In the systematic review and meta-analysis of 13 trials, aspirin use was associated with an increased risk of major bleeding events compared with no aspirin (23.1 per 10,000 participant-years with aspirin and 16.4 per 10,000 participant-years with no aspirin; HR, 1.43 [95% credible interval, 1.30-1.56]; absolute risk increase, 0.47% [95% CI, 0.34%-0.62%]; number needed to harm, 210).

evidence.quote: Aspirin use was associated with an increased risk of major bleeding events compared with no aspirin (23.1 per 10 000 participant-years with aspirin and 16.4 per 10 000 participant-years with no aspirin) (HR, 1.43 [95% credible interval, 1.30-1.56]; absolute risk increase, 0.47% [95% CI, 0.34%-0.62%]; number needed to harm, 210).

claims.text: In ARRIVE, gastrointestinal bleeding events (mostly mild) occurred in 61 (0.97%) patients in the aspirin group versus 29 (0.46%) in the placebo group (HR 2.11; 95% CI 1.36-3.28; p=0.0007).

evidence.quote: Gastrointestinal bleeding events (mostly mild) occurred in 61 (0·97%) patients in the aspirin group versus 29 (0·46%) in the placebo group (HR 2·11; 95% CI 1·36-3·28; p=0·0007).

claims.text: In ASCEND, major bleeding events occurred in 314 participants (4.1%) in the aspirin group, as compared with 245 (3.2%) in the placebo group (rate ratio, 1.29; 95% CI, 1.09 to 1.52; P=0.003), with most of the excess being gastrointestinal bleeding and other extracranial bleeding.

evidence.quote: In contrast, major bleeding events occurred in 314 participants (4.1%) in the aspirin group, as compared with 245 (3.2%) in the placebo group (rate ratio, 1.29; 95% CI, 1.09 to 1.52; P=0.003), with most of the excess being gastrointestinal bleeding and other extracranial bleeding.

claims.text: In ASPREE, the rate of major hemorrhage was 8.6 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 6.2 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (HR, 1.38; 95% CI, 1.18 to 1.62; P<0.001).

evidence.quote: The rate of major hemorrhage was 8.6 events per 1000 person-years and 6.2 events per 1000 person-years, respectively (hazard ratio, 1.38; 95% CI, 1.18 to 1.62; P<0.001).

claims.text: The 2009 collaborative meta-analysis concluded that in primary prevention without previous disease, aspirin is of uncertain net value as the reduction in occlusive events needs to be weighed against any increase in major bleeds.

evidence.quote: In primary prevention without previous disease, aspirin is of uncertain net value as the reduction in occlusive events needs to be weighed against any increase in major bleeds.

claims.text: The 2019 systematic review concluded that the use of aspirin in individuals without cardiovascular disease was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events and an increased risk of major bleeding.

evidence.quote: The use of aspirin in individuals without cardiovascular disease was associated with a lower risk of cardiovascular events and an increased risk of major bleeding.

claims.text: In ASCEND, aspirin use prevented serious vascular events in persons who had diabetes and no evident cardiovascular disease at trial entry, but it also caused major bleeding events, and the absolute benefits were largely counterbalanced by the bleeding hazard.

evidence.quote: Aspirin use prevented serious vascular events in persons who had diabetes and no evident cardiovascular disease at trial entry, but it also caused major bleeding events. The absolute benefits were largely counterbalanced by the bleeding hazard.

claims.text: In ASPREE, the use of low-dose aspirin as a primary prevention strategy in older adults resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and did not result in a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo.

evidence.quote: The use of low-dose aspirin as a primary prevention strategy in older adults resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and did not result in a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo.

claims.text: Across the primary prevention trials, the direction of the findings is consistent — a modest reduction in cardiovascular events and an increase in major bleeding — while the trials differ in population and design, including moderate-risk adults (ARRIVE), adults with diabetes (ASCEND), older adults (ASPREE) and older Japanese adults with atherosclerotic risk factors (JPPP).

evidence.quote: In the intention-to-treat analysis, the primary endpoint occurred in 269 (4·29%) patients in the aspirin group versus 281 (4·48%) patients in the placebo group (hazard ratio [HR] 0·96; 95% CI 0·81-1·13; p=0·6038).
Aspirin use prevented serious vascular events in persons who had diabetes and no evident cardiovascular disease at trial entry, but it also caused major bleeding events.

The use of low-dose aspirin as a primary prevention strategy in older adults resulted in a significantly higher risk of major hemorrhage and did not result in a significantly lower risk of cardiovascular disease than placebo.

The 5-year cumulative primary outcome event rate was not significantly different between the groups (2.77% [95% CI, 2.40%-3.20%] for aspirin vs 2.96% [95% CI, 2.58%-3.40%] for no aspirin; hazard ratio [HR], 0.94 [95% CI, 0.77-1.15]; P = .54).

sections.heading: All-cause and cancer mortality in older adults

claims.text: In ASPREE, the risk of death from any cause was 12.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.1 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (HR, 1.14; 95% CI, 1.01 to 1.29).

evidence.quote: The risk of death from any cause was 12.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.1 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.14; 95% confidence interval [CI], 1.01 to 1.29).

claims.text: In ASPREE, cancer was the major contributor to the higher mortality in the aspirin group, accounting for 1.6 excess deaths per 1000 person-years, and cancer-related death occurred in 3.1% of participants in the aspirin group and 2.3% of those in the placebo group (HR, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.10 to 1.56).

evidence.quote: Cancer was the major contributor to the higher mortality in the aspirin group, accounting for 1.6 excess deaths per 1000 person-years. Cancer-related death occurred in 3.1% of the participants in the aspirin group and in 2.3% of those in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 1.31; 95% CI, 1.10 to 1.56).

claims.text: The ASPREE investigators stated that the higher all-cause mortality observed among apparently healthy older adults who received daily aspirin was unexpected in the context of previous studies and should be interpreted with caution.

evidence.quote: Higher all-cause mortality was observed among apparently healthy older adults who received daily aspirin than among those who received placebo and was attributed primarily to cancer-related death. In the context of previous studies, this result was unexpected and should be interpreted with caution.

claims.text: In ASCEND, there was no significant difference between the aspirin group and the placebo group in the incidence of gastrointestinal tract cancer (157 participants [2.0%] and 158 [2.0%], respectively) or all cancers (897 [11.6%] and 887 [11.5%]).

evidence.quote: There was no significant difference between the aspirin group and the placebo group in the incidence of gastrointestinal tract cancer (157 participants [2.0%] and 158 [2.0%], respectively) or all cancers (897 [11.6%] and 887 [11.5%]); long-term follow-up for these outcomes is planned.

claims.text: The ASPREE mortality finding and the ASCEND cancer-incidence finding point in different directions, and the two trials differ in population and in the outcome examined (all-cause and cancer mortality versus incident cancer).

evidence.quote: Higher all-cause mortality was observed among apparently healthy older adults who received daily aspirin than among those who received placebo and was attributed primarily to cancer-related death.

There was no significant difference between the aspirin group and the placebo group in the incidence of gastrointestinal tract cancer (157 participants [2.0%] and 158 [2.0%], respectively) or all cancers (897 [11.6%] and 887 [11.5%]); long-term follow-up for these outcomes is planned.

claims.text: The US Preventive Services Task Force concludes with moderate certainty that aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk has a small net benefit.

evidence.quote: The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk has a small net benefit.

claims.text: The US Preventive Services Task Force concludes with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit.

evidence.quote: The USPSTF concludes with moderate certainty that initiating aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD events in adults 60 years or older has no net benefit.

claims.text: The USPSTF recommends that the decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one, and recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older.

evidence.quote: The decision to initiate low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults aged 40 to 59 years who have a 10% or greater 10-year CVD risk should be an individual one. … The USPSTF recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin use for the primary prevention of CVD in adults 60 years or older. (D recommendation).

claims.text: The USPSTF population for this recommendation is adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD who are not at increased risk for bleeding.

evidence.quote: Adults 40 years or older without signs or symptoms of CVD or known CVD (including history of myocardial infarction or stroke) who are not at increased risk for bleeding (eg, no history of gastrointestinal ulcers, recent bleeding, other medical conditions, or use of medications that increase bleeding risk).

claims.text: ARRIVE was a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre study done in seven countries, in which eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk deemed moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors.

evidence.quote: ARRIVE is a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled, multicentre study done in seven countries. Eligible patients were aged 55 years (men) or 60 years (women) and older and had an average cardiovascular risk, deemed to be moderate on the basis of the number of specific risk factors.

claims.text: ARRIVE excluded patients at high risk of gastrointestinal bleeding or other bleeding, or diabetes, and randomly assigned patients 1:1 to enteric-coated aspirin tablets (100 mg) or placebo tablets, once daily.

evidence.quote: We excluded patients at high risk of gastrointestinal bleeding or other bleeding, or diabetes. Patients were randomly assigned (1:1) with a computer-generated randomisation code to receive enteric-coated aspirin tablets (100 mg) or placebo tablets, once daily.

claims.text: The primary efficacy endpoint of ARRIVE was a composite outcome of time to first occurrence of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, unstable angina, stroke, or transient ischaemic attack.

evidence.quote: The primary efficacy endpoint was a composite outcome of time to first occurrence of cardiovascular death, myocardial infarction, unstable angina, stroke, or transient ischaemic attack.

claims.text: Between July 5, 2007, and Nov 15, 2016, 12,546 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive aspirin (n=6270) or placebo (n=6276) at 501 study sites, with a median follow-up of 60 months.

evidence.quote: Between July 5, 2007, and Nov 15, 2016, 12 546 patients were enrolled and randomly assigned to receive aspirin (n=6270) or placebo (n=6276) at 501 study sites. Median follow-up was 60 months.

claims.text: In ARRIVE, the overall incidence rate of serious adverse events was similar in both treatment groups (n=1266 [20.19%] in the aspirin group vs n=1311 [20.89%] in the placebo group), and there were 321 documented deaths in the intention-to-treat population (n=160 [2.55%] vs n=161 [2.57%] of 6276 patients in the placebo group).

evidence.quote: The overall incidence rate of serious adverse events was similar in both treatment groups (n=1266 [20·19%] in the aspirin group vs n=1311 [20·89%] in the placebo group.

claims.text: ASCEND randomly assigned adults who had diabetes but no evident cardiovascular disease to receive aspirin at a dose of 100 mg daily or matching placebo.

evidence.quote: We randomly assigned adults who had diabetes but no evident cardiovascular disease to receive aspirin at a dose of 100 mg daily or matching placebo.

claims.text: The primary efficacy outcome of ASCEND was the first serious vascular event (myocardial infarction, stroke or transient ischemic attack, or death from any vascular cause, excluding any confirmed intracranial hemorrhage), and the primary safety outcome was the first major bleeding event.

evidence.quote: The primary efficacy outcome was the first serious vascular event (i.e., myocardial infarction, stroke or transient ischemic attack, or death from any vascular cause, excluding any confirmed intracranial hemorrhage). The primary safety outcome was the first major bleeding event (i.e., intracranial hemorrhage, sight-threatening bleeding event in the eye, gastrointestinal bleeding, or other serious bleeding).

claims.text: A total of 15,480 participants underwent randomization in ASCEND, with a mean follow-up of 7.4 years.

evidence.quote: A total of 15,480 participants underwent randomization. During a mean follow-up of 7.4 years, serious vascular events occurred in a significantly lower percentage of participants in the aspirin group than in the placebo group (658 participants [8.5%] vs. 743 [9.6%]; rate ratio, 0.88; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.79 to 0.97; P=0.01).

claims.text: From 2010 through 2014, ASPREE enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability, randomly assigned to receive 100 mg of enteric-coated aspirin or placebo.

evidence.quote: From 2010 through 2014, we enrolled community-dwelling men and women in Australia and the United States who were 70 years of age or older (or ≥65 years of age among blacks and Hispanics in the United States) and did not have cardiovascular disease, dementia, or disability. Participants were randomly assigned to receive 100 mg of enteric-coated aspirin or placebo.

claims.text: The primary end point of ASPREE was a composite of death, dementia, or persistent physical disability, and secondary end points included major hemorrhage and cardiovascular disease.

evidence.quote: The primary end point was a composite of death, dementia, or persistent physical disability; results for this end point are reported in another article in the Journal. Secondary end points included major hemorrhage and cardiovascular disease (defined as fatal coronary heart disease, nonfatal myocardial infarction, fatal or nonfatal stroke, or hospitalization for heart failure).

claims.text: Of the 19,114 persons enrolled in ASPREE, 9525 were assigned to receive aspirin and 9589 to receive placebo, with a median of 4.7 years of follow-up.

evidence.quote: Of the 19,114 persons who were enrolled in the trial, 9525 were assigned to receive aspirin and 9589 to receive placebo. After a median of 4.7 years of follow-up, the rate of cardiovascular disease was 10.7 events per 1000 person-years in the aspirin group and 11.3 events per 1000 person-years in the placebo group (hazard ratio, 0.95; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.83 to 1.08).

claims.text: A total of 1052 deaths occurred during a median of 4.7 years of follow-up in ASPREE, and deaths were classified according to the underlying cause by adjudicators who were unaware of trial-group assignments.

evidence.quote: A total of 1052 deaths occurred during a median of 4.7 years of follow-up.

claims.text: The Japanese Primary Prevention Project was a multicenter, open-label, randomized, parallel-group trial in which patients (N = 14,464) aged 60 to 85 years with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus were recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007 and followed up for up to 6.5 years.

evidence.quote: The Japanese Primary Prevention Project (JPPP) was a multicenter, open-label, randomized, parallel-group trial. Patients (N = 14,464) were aged 60 to 85 years, presenting with hypertension, dyslipidemia, or diabetes mellitus recruited by primary care physicians at 1007 clinics in Japan between March 2005 and June 2007, and were followed up for up to 6.5 years, with last follow-up in May 2012.

claims.text: Patients in JPPP were randomized 1:1 to enteric-coated aspirin 100 mg/d or no aspirin in addition to ongoing medications, and a multidisciplinary expert panel blinded to treatment assignments adjudicated study outcomes.

evidence.quote: Patients were randomized 1:1 to enteric-coated aspirin 100 mg/d or no aspirin in addition to ongoing medications.

claims.text: JPPP was terminated early by the data monitoring committee after a median follow-up of 5.02 years (interquartile range, 4.55-5.33) based on likely futility.

evidence.quote: The study was terminated early by the data monitoring committee after a median follow-up of 5.02 years (interquartile range, 4.55-5.33) based on likely futility.

claims.text: In JPPP, 56 fatal events occurred in both the aspirin and no aspirin groups, nonfatal stroke occurred in 114 patients in the aspirin group and 108 in the no aspirin group, and nonfatal myocardial infarction occurred in 20 in the aspirin group and 38 in the no aspirin group.

evidence.quote: In both the aspirin and no aspirin groups, 56 fatal events occurred. Patients with an occurrence of nonfatal stroke totaled 114 in the aspirin group and 108 in the no aspirin group; of nonfatal myocardial infarction, 20 in the aspirin group and 38 in the no aspirin group; of undefined cerebrovascular events, 3 in the aspirin group and 5 in the no aspirin group.

claims.text: To update its 2016 recommendation, the USPSTF commissioned a systematic review on the effectiveness of aspirin to reduce the risk of CVD events, cardiovascular mortality, and all-cause mortality in persons without a history of CVD, and a microsimulation modeling study to assess the net balance of benefits and harms from aspirin use for primary prevention of CVD and CRC, stratified by age, sex, and CVD risk level.

evidence.quote: To update its 2016 recommendation, the US Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) commissioned a systematic review on the effectiveness of aspirin to reduce the risk of CVD events (myocardial infarction and stroke), cardiovascular mortality, and all-cause mortality in persons without a history of CVD. … The USPSTF also commissioned a microsimulation modeling study to assess the net balance of benefits and harms from aspirin use for primary prevention of CVD and CRC, stratified by age, sex, and CVD risk level.

claims.text: The USPSTF states that persons who are not at increased risk for bleeding and are willing to take low-dose aspirin daily are more likely to benefit.

evidence.quote: Persons who are not at increased risk for bleeding and are willing to take low-dose aspirin daily are more likely to benefit. (C recommendation)

lint.note: ASPREE reported higher all-cause mortality with aspirin, attributed primarily to cancer-related death, while ASCEND found no significant difference in incident gastrointestinal tract cancer or all cancers; the trials differ in population and in the outcome examined, so both findings are kept.

The 2009 collaborative meta-analysis found a 12% proportional reduction in serious vascular events with aspirin in primary prevention, whereas the later individual trials (ARRIVE, JPPP, ASPREE) found no significant reduction in their primary composite endpoints; populations and endpoint definitions differ, so both are kept.
The 2022 USPSTF statement updates the 2016 recommendation and recommends against initiating low-dose aspirin for primary prevention in adults 60 years or older.
